A pay rise that matches inflation needs a tax-threshold check before you reset the budget

Read CRA’s published indexation adjustments, then use five charts to separate nominal pay, marginal tax thresholds and annual income in constant purchasing-power units.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two hypothetical threshold rules and income purchasing power

Interactive planning lab

Final annual gross income in starting-year purchasing power$80,000
Final annual net income with inflation-indexed thresholds, starting-year CAD$61,000
Final annual net-income gap: indexed less fixed thresholds, starting-year CAD$1,838.59

The first chart reproduces CRA’s dated annual indexation percentages for 2023–2026, reviewed 25 October 2026. They are not annual-average CPI inflation readings or future forecasts. The remaining four charts are an independent teaching model, not a Canadian tax calculator or a forecast of policy. Its constructed marginal rates are 20% on the first CAD 50,000, 30% on the next CAD 50,000 and 40% above CAD 100,000 in the starting year. There is no tax-free amount, credit, deduction, payroll contribution, provincial calculation, benefit or other income. All entered income is taxable. One rule holds both thresholds fixed; the other multiplies both by the same cumulative price factor used to deflate income. Rates stay constant and thresholds are not rounded. Each year’s nominal income grows by the selected pay rate. Annual net income means gross income less this illustrative tax only, not actual take-home pay or an accumulated savings balance. There is no investment return or payment-date calculation.

The central idea

Equal percentage increases in pay and prices preserve gross purchasing power. The tax schedule determines how that comparison carries through to net income.

01

Put pay, prices and thresholds on the same calendar

A salary can rise without buying more. A tax bracket can also change even when its percentage rate stays the same. A household budget therefore needs three separate records: nominal income, the prices it must pay and the tax rules applying to that income year.

The CRA rate page explains that each marginal rate applies to its corresponding income slice. Moving into a higher slice does not apply that rate to every dollar. The threshold identifies where the next rate begins; the rate tells you how that slice is taxed.

The interactive example isolates thresholds. It deliberately uses a constructed schedule rather than estimating a Canadian return. Actual planning requires the applicable federal and provincial or territorial rules, credits, deductions and other payroll items.

02

Read the official adjustment series before choosing a future assumption

CRA’s indexation table reports increases of 6.3% for 2023, 4.7% for 2024, 2.7% for 2025 and 2.0% for 2026. These are the published indexation adjustments, not a series of household pay rises or annual-average CPI inflation rates.

The page explains that certain personal income tax and benefit amounts are indexed using Statistics Canada CPI data. The relevant amount and its effective date still matter. Do not infer that every tax parameter or benefit follows one identical rule.

The first chart stays fixed as you edit the scenario. The model’s default 3% price increase is a separate assumption for an unnamed future period. It does not extend the four official observations into a forecast.

03

Use a small invented schedule to see the threshold effect

In the starting year, the teaching schedule taxes the first CAD 50,000 at 20%, the next CAD 50,000 at 30% and income above CAD 100,000 at 40%. It has no tax-free amount, credits, deductions or payroll contributions. These are not Canadian federal, provincial or combined tax brackets.

At CAD 80,000 of starting income, illustrative tax is CAD 10,000 on the first slice plus CAD 9,000 on the second. Annual net income is CAD 61,000. The 30% marginal rate applies to the second slice; it is not the average rate on all CAD 80,000.

Both modeled rules start from that exact schedule. One keeps CAD 50,000 and CAD 100,000 fixed. The other increases both thresholds by the cumulative assumed price factor, retaining the same rates and omitting rounding. Nothing else changes between the rules.

04

Deflate annual net income after calculating each year’s tax

The nominal income path is starting income multiplied by one plus the pay increase for each elapsed year. The price factor compounds separately. Divide each year’s nominal gross or net income by its price factor to express it in starting-year purchasing power.

With the default 3% pay increase and 3% price increase, real gross income remains CAD 80,000. Under the fully indexed constructed thresholds, real annual net income remains CAD 61,000. Income and both thresholds scale together, so the same income proportions face the same rates.

At year 10, the default nominal income is about CAD 107,513.31. Fixed thresholds leave annual net income worth about CAD 59,161.41 in starting-year dollars, compared with CAD 61,000 under indexed thresholds. The annual purchasing-power difference is about CAD 1,838.59.

Under fixed thresholds, more of the inflation-adjusted salary increase can enter higher nominal slices. This effect is often called bracket creep. A real pay increase can still improve net purchasing power despite that effect; the comparison must retain the actual pay assumption. Full threshold indexation alone does not guarantee a household’s expenses, benefits or actual take-home income move in step.

05

Keep annual income, nominal dollars and accumulated savings distinct

The stacked bars divide final-year nominal income into tax and net income. Each bar has the same total gross salary. The line chart instead shows annual net income in starting-year dollars, making the purchasing-power comparison visible.

The waterfall begins with indexed-threshold real net income and subtracts the fixed-threshold tax difference in the same units. Its endpoint matches the fixed-threshold line. The difference is one selected year’s annual income gap; it is not an accumulated ten-year loss or a separate bill.

The matrix changes pay and price growth independently while retaining starting income and the horizon. A larger gap between the two rules does not, by itself, prove that the household has become poorer than it was initially. For that question, compare each real net-income result with the starting value as well.

06

Translate the explanation into a budget update

For a real pay review, record the new gross amount and effective date, estimate the applicable tax and payroll deductions, and check the actual net deposits. Compare those deposits with the household’s own changed bills. A national price measure provides context but cannot price every family’s basket.

Then decide how much of the verified monthly change can support saving, debt repayment or additional spending. A nominal pay percentage is too early in that chain to become a recurring spending commitment on its own.

The official series explains an existing indexation mechanism. The two invented rules explain why thresholds matter. Neither establishes future legislation, a personal tax liability, benefit entitlement or the timing of cash received.
